Examines embedded and cyber physical systems design requirements and specifications. Reviews embedded and cyber physical systems emerging applications through a class project. Prerequisite: COE 241; prerequisite/concurrent: ELE 340.

COE 420.d: Introduces the basic principles and practices of software engineering. Emphasizes the different phases of the software development process and quality issues. Includes the following topics: software life cycle models; general design, implementation and testing issues; specification and design methodologies; model-based approaches to software design; project management; and the use of various design and development tools. Prerequisite: CMP 305.

COE 421L.d: Covers the main activities that make up the development lifecycle of a complex computer system including requirement engineering, architectural design, design patterns, configuration management, and verification and validation. Follows a project-based learning approach to offer a hands-on experience in building computer systems using contemporary software engineering methods and tools. Prerequisite/concurrent: CMP 310.

COE 425.d: Covers performance measures, RISC processors, datapath and control units design, memory hierarchy, pipelining, I/O systems and multiprocessors. Prerequisite: COE 341.

COE 428.d: Covers CMOS technology, layout rules and techniques, CMOS logic and circuit design, circuit characterization and performance estimation, and design methodologies and tools. Prerequisites: COE 221 and ELE 241.

COE 431.d: Covers the conceptual model and layers of cyber physical systems (CPS); the industrial applications in CPS of microprocessor-based data acquisition units and programmable logic controllers; web-based monitoring and control of industrial plants; and recent developments in industrial automation. Includes class projects. Prerequisite: COE 411.

COE 434.d: Covers wireless communications and networks, location management, routing in ad hoc wireless network, file systems issues and caching strategies. Prerequisite: COE 371.

COE 444.d: Covers a broad variety of topics in computer security. Includes the following topics: authentication and authorization, introduction and application of cryptography, social engineering attacks, physical security, network security, application security (web, e-mail), wireless security, operating system security, intrusion detection systems and firewalls, program security, security management, block chain technologies, and ethical and legal issues in computer security. Prerequisite: COE 371.

COE 457.d: Focuses on Internet and Internet of Things (IoT) programming. Topics include programming using Internet and IoT protocols, advanced JavaScript programming, NSQL databases, crossplatform web-application development, and architectures for Internet of Things. Prerequisites: COE 371 and CMP 310.

COE 476.d: Covers tensors, neural network modelling, gradient descent optimization and loss functions, feature engineering, and evaluation of neural networks. Focusses on various types of neural networks including feedforward networks, auto-encoders, convolutional neural networks and recurrent neural networks. Discusses topics in generative deep learning. Prerequisites: CMP 305 and MTH 221.

COE 487.d: Focuses on hardware and software aspects of virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) systems. Addresses the integration of AR and VR technologies in the development of computer games and other engineering applications. Covers 3D modeling, inertial measurement units (IMUs) and sensors, scene management, user interactivity, performance evaluation, single and multiplayer games, and use of patterns in game development. Prerequisites: CMP 305 and MTH 221.

COE 490.d: Covers the engineering design process through an open-ended, team-based project of disciplinary relevance. Applies disciplinespecific methods and tools to problem identification, definition of objectives and constraints, evaluation of alternatives, and development of a preliminary design. Addresses factors such as sustainability, safety, ethics, economics, societal impact and standards in the design process. Emphasizes the aspects of innovation, entrepreneurship and intellectual property. Develops professional teamwork and communication skills. Not open to computer science students. Prerequisites: COE 371, ENG 204 and senior standing; prerequisites/concurrent: IEN 301, and COE 420 or COE 421L.

COE 491.d: Continues the work of COE 490. Emphasizes the application of engineering principles to solve real-world problems. Includes exposure to industry practices through interaction with companies or professionals. Prerequisite: COE 490.

COE 497.d: Provides opportunities for the application of computer engineering knowledge and skills to actual problems in a real-life work setting. Enhances learning and soft skills through practical experience. Reinforces objective-setting and performance measurement through a structured reporting process. Requires a minimum of 16 weeks of approved professional experience of on-the-job training. Graded as Pass/No Pass. Prerequisites: ENG 204, junior standing and approval of internship coordinator. CVE Civil Engineering

CVE 111.d: Introduces graphical communication including lettering, drawing equipment and techniques. Covers orthographic projections, sections and technical sketching. Uses isometric and oblique drawings for communication and documentation of engineering design. Employs computer-aided design tools.

CVE 202.d: Focuses on the application of basic measurement techniques and instrumentation to the experimental investigation of construction materials: aggregate, bitumen, pavement materials, asphalt mixes, cement, concrete materials, concrete mixes, mild and high tensile steel testing, non-destructive testing. Includes timber and metals tests. Requires written reports covering the planning, execution, results and conclusions of the investigation. Emphasizes teamwork. Prerequisite/concurrent: CVE 224.

CVE 222.d: Covers fundamental concepts and principles of mechanics, vectors and force systems; free-body-diagram; equilibrium principles of particles and rigid bodies; analysis of structures; shear and bending moment; center of gravity, centroids, area and mass moments of inertia; friction; kinetics of rigid bodies; Single-Degree-OfFreedom (SDOF) vibrations. Prerequisites: PHY 101 and PHY 101L.

CVE 223.d: (Equivalent to MCE 223). Covers stress and strains; mechanical properties of materials; axial load, torsion, bending and transverse shear; combined loading; stress transformation; deflection of beams and shafts; and buckling of columns. Prerequisite: CVE 222 or MCE 220 or MCE 224.

CVE 224.d: Examines properties of construction materials (aggregate, Portland cement, admixtures, concrete and bituminous materials used in construction and maintenance of structures, roads and pavements); design of concrete mixes including admixtures; concrete trial mixes on construction site; concrete curing methods; concrete strength and durability; design of paving Undergraduate Course Descriptions mixtures; and production, specifications, tests and quality control of various construction materials. Prerequisites: CVE 223, CHM 101 and CHM 101L; prerequisite/concurrent: CVE 202.

CVE 232.d: Covers the nature and structure of earth, formation of rocks, chemical and physical properties of minerals, weathering, volcanoes, earthquakes and tectonic movements, types of mountains and their formation, groundwater and surface water processes and contamination, rock mass instabilities, and global climate change. Prerequisite: NGN 110.

CVE 240.d: Examines foundational principles of fluid mechanics by emphasizing fluid properties, pressure measurement, hydrostatic forces and the stability of floating bodies. Covers major topics such as fluid kinematics, velocity and acceleration fields, the application of the Euler equation, laminar and turbulent flow regimes, dimensional analysis, dynamic similitude and boundary layer development. Applies Reynolds Transport Theorem to derive the integral conservation equations for continuity, momentum and energy. Uses these governing equations to analyze pipe systems, including series and parallel configurations and methods of computing energy losses. Prerequisites: CVE 222 and MTH 104.

CVE 243.d: Covers basic geomatics principles and applications, with a focus on data acquisition, processing and analysis. Includes measurement techniques, error theory, traversing, topographic mapping, area and earthwork calculations, spatial datum and reference systems. Introduces state-of-the-art geospatial technologies and data analysis techniques, including GNSS, remote sensing, LiDAR mapping, GIS and GeoAI. Provides hands-on skills in using geomatics tools and applying spatial data analysis techniques to real-world civil engineering problems through field and laboratory exercises. Prerequisites: MTH 104 and NGN 112.

CVE 263.d: Examines urban transportation system planning techniques: data collection, trip generation, trip distribution, factors underlying the choice of mode, traffic assignment, modeling and evaluation techniques, use of planning software packages, development of alternatives, and evaluation of civil engineering projects. Introduces Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS). Prerequisites: CVE 243 and NGN 211.

CVE 267.d: Covers economic analysis and evaluation of civil engineering proposals utilizing time-value and related factors, time value of money, worth of investments and economic evaluation of alternative choices, replacement and retention decisions, selection from independent projects, inflation, cost estimating fundamentals, parametric cost estimating, probabilistic cost estimating, depreciation, breakeven analysis and benefit cost analysis. Prerequisite: NGN 211.

CVE 301.d: Covers stability and determinacy of structures; force calculation in trusses; axial load, shear and bending moment diagrams for beams and frames; approximate analysis of indeterminate frames; analysis of cables and arches; deflection calculations; influence lines for determinate structures; and analysis of statically indeterminate structures using classical methods. Uses commercial software for structural analysis. Prerequisite: CVE 223.

CVE 303.d: Includes experiments in soil mechanics. Laboratory experiments cover geotechnical test equipment and techniques. Includes the applications of testing principles to the measurement of fundamental aspects of soil behavior from classification to engineering properties. Emphasizes rigorous techniques to measure mechanical behavior under various boundary conditions. Provides exposure to error estimation. Utilizes standard test methods and equipment to assess physical, mechanical, chemical and hydraulic properties of soils for application in civil engineering design. Includes laboratory work on classification and engineering tests on intact and weathered rock. Prerequisite: NGN 211; prerequisite/concurrent: CVE 331.

CVE 312.d: Covers loads on structures, design criteria and philosophies, and analysis and design of structural steel elements found in buildings and bridges including tension members, compression members, beams, columns, beam columns and connections. Requires a design project and use of computer software. Prerequisite: CVE 301.

CVE 313.d: Covers loads on structures; design criteria and factors of safety; analysis and design of reinforced concrete beams, short columns, one-way slabs and footings using ultimate strength method; and bond development of reinforcement. Requires a design project and use of computer software. Prerequisites: CVE 224 and CVE 301.

CVE 325.d: (Equivalent to MCE 325). Covers basic concepts of computational methods; numerical solution of non-linear equations; iterative methods for solving systems of linear Undergraduate Course Descriptions algebraic equations; numerical differentiation and integration; interpolation; and curve fitting. Includes numerical solutions of ordinary differential equations. Introduces various probability distribution functions, and covers uncertainty and risk analysis in engineering applications. Includes applications of computational methods using computers. Prerequisites: NGN 112, NGN 211 and MTH 225.

CVE 331.d: Studies physical properties of soils, classification systems, soil structure and soil water systems, effective stress principle and stresses in soil due to applied loads. Includes the following topics: compressibility, consolidation and swell; permeability and seepage analysis; soil compaction; stressstrain-shear strength relationships of soils; failure criteria; direct and triaxial shear testing; and soils used in construction. Introduces lateral earth pressures. Uses computer software for geotechnical analysis. Prerequisites: CVE 223 and CVE 232; prerequisite/concurrent: CVE 303.

CVE 333.d: Covers subsurface exploration and site investigation and evaluation; bearing capacity of shallow foundations in different types of soils; settlement analysis (consolidation and immediate); design of shallow foundations including footings and raftings; design of deep foundations including driven piles, shafts and drilled piers; pile load tests; end bearing and friction of deep foundations under axial loading; settlement of piles; bearing capacity and settlement of pile groups; piles subjected to lateral loading and moments; and design of pile foundations. Introduces design of retaining walls. Requires extensive use of computer-aided design in team projects. Prerequisite: CVE 331.

CVE 341.d: Introduces flow of water through pipes and channels, over the ground surface, and through the subsurface. Covers incompressible flow in pipes, methods of energy loss computations, pumps, steady flow in pipe networks, and design of pipe networks using computer applications. Includes open channel hydraulics, design of water supply canals, bridge and culvert hydraulics, and open channel flow modeling. Introduces surface hydrology including runoff modeling. Covers subsurface flow and wells hydraulics. Includes team projects, and analysis and design using computer software. Prerequisite: CVE 240.

CVE 352.d: Introduces environmental engineering and sustainability. Covers materials balance, reaction kinetics and reactor theory. Introduces water quality parameters, modeling and source assessment. Covers planning and design of water and wastewater treatment processes, and sustainable solid waste planning and management. Introduces laboratory assessments of water quality parameters and treatment methods. Prerequisites: CHM 101 and CHM 101L, and CVE 240 or MCE 240 or CHE 300.

CVE 363.d: Explores driver and vehicle characteristics, stopping and passing sight distances, cross section elements, vertical and horizontal alignment, intersections and interchanges, surface drainage, types of pavements, and principles, theoretical concepts and design of flexible and rigid pavements. Prerequisite: CVE 263.

CVE 367.d: Covers the application of cost estimating and planning techniques for construction projects. Introduces construction project management; quantity surveying; labor, material and equipment costing; indirect and general overhead costs; preparation of approximate and definitive estimates; work breakdown structures; project scheduling; network modeling; critical path method; program evaluation and review techniques; timecost tradeoff; earned value; project controls and project closeout. Prerequisite: CVE 267.

CVE 410.d: Introduces matrix algebra, degrees of freedom and system coordinates. Explores virtual work method, stiffness and flexibility methods, matrix formulation of the stiffness and flexibility methods, direct stiffness method, introduction to finite element method, computer analysis of 2D and 3D framed structures. Emphasizes team-based learning through projects. Prerequisites: CVE 301, and MTH 221 or MTH 225.

CVE 411.d: Introduces flooring and structural systems. Covers design of reinforced concrete members including beams subjected to torsion, two-way slabs, column under biaxial bending, slender columns, combined footings and shear walls. Introduces pre-stressed concrete, pre-stress materials and losses. Includes design of pre-stressed beams and computer analysis and design of structures. Emphasizes team-based learning through specific design projects. Prerequisite: CVE 313.

CVE 414.d: Covers the analysis and design requirements for prestressed concrete members; materials, prestressing systems and methods; prestress losses; flexural design for service stresses at transfer and at service; ultimate flexural and shear strength design; composite construction and secondary moments. Prerequisite: CVE 313.

CVE 441.d: Covers wave theories and their characteristics; wave transformation (wave refraction, diffraction and reflection); wave forces and concepts and theories of wave structure interactions; water level fluctuations (tides); coastal and ocean structures; design of seawalls, breakwater and shore protection systems; design of selected coastal structures; and hydraulic considerations. Introduces selected coastal engineering problems. Prerequisite: CVE 341.

CVE 442.d: Includes site investigation with emphasis on in-situ testing. Covers interpretation of field and laboratory data; design of retaining structures, braced excavations, sheet-pile walls and reinforced earth structures; and the design of staged construction embankments and slopes. Introduces seismic behavior of ground and geotechnical earthquake engineering. Emphasizes design of locally used geotechnical structures. Prerequisite: CVE 331.

CVE 446.d: Examines regional geoscience and seismotectonic investigations; selection type of dam; related geophysical subsurface exploration seepage in composite sections, anisotropic and multilayered materials; dams stability analysis; design of dam foundations; foundation treatment; and grouting in the ground. Introduces earthquake analysis and design of earth and rock-fill dams. Special considerations include liquefaction problems, sinkholes, land subsidence, foundation defects and dispersive soils. Covers monitoring and staged construction and evaluates the ecological and geo-environmental effect of the dam construction. Prerequisite/concurrent: CVE 331.

CVE 451.d: Introduces drinking water, wastewater and stormwater infrastructures. Includes water quality management of water infrastructures, waste solids handling and disposal practices and integrity of water infrastructures, design approach and construction of infrastructure, and operations, maintenance and renewal of water, sewer and stormwater systems. Introduces financial management, asset management, risk management and the use of information technology in water management. Prerequisites/concurrent: CVE 341 and CVE 352.

CVE 452.d: Introduces water demand, water supply sources, water use trends and forecasting. Includes fundamentals of surface water and groundwater collection and transportation; design of wells and water distribution systems; estimation of industrial, domestic and fire demands; water meters; and leak detection. Identifies processes for sustainable water use and economics of water supply. Covers wastewater generation, construction and maintenance of sanitary sewer and plumbing systems in buildings. Prerequisite/concurrent: CVE 341.

CVE 456.d: Explores characteristics of road users and the characteristics of the traffic stream: speed-flow-density, traffic volume, traffic accidents, travel time and delay, parking, capacity and level of service of freeways, signalized intersections and at-grade intersection design. Covers transportation models. Prerequisite: CVE 263.

CVE 457.d: Examines airport master planning, forecasting air travel demand and design of airports, including lighting, terminal facilities, noise-level control, aircraft control, airspace utilization and automobile parking. Prerequisite: CVE 263.

CVE 460.d: Introduces fundamentals of managing components/processes/impacts of transport systems: travel demand and travel time impacts and management, environmental impacts (air quality, noise, water) and management, safety systems management, public health impacts and management, transport system operations and control, transportation asset management, and pavement management systems. Covers applicable metrics, performance measures and evaluation methods with a focus on sustainability. Prerequisite: CVE 263.

CVE 461.d: Focuses on transit systems planning methods in urban areas. Covers analysis, evaluation and selection of transit modes with focus on the twin themes of sustainability and innovation. Examines operational issues regarding lines, stops, networks, stations, vehicles, transit units, and fleet size. Prerequisite: CVE 263.

CVE 463.d: Examines management in the construction industry; construction delivery systems; management organizations; construction contracts; preconstruction planning and scheduling; bidding and award; contract administration and control; managing submittals, drawings, communications, progress payments, cash flow and site materials; and progress monitoring and control. Introduces construction quality and safety management. Prerequisite: CVE 367. Undergraduate Course Descriptions finishes. Prerequisites: CVE 111 and CVE 267.

CVE 467.d: Covers traditional and alternative building systems, the principles, materials, methods, codes and standards, and discusses their advantages and limitations. Encompasses aspects of site preparation, excavation and formwork, foundation choices, different elements of frame construction, scaffolding, thermal and moisture protection, electrical wiring, heating ventilation and air-conditioning (HVAC), plumbing, roofing, cladding systems, and external and internal

CVE 472.d: Introduces the concept and use of Geographic Information Systems (GIS). Covers assorted topics in GIS including map generation and analysis, vector and raster GIS, spatial databases and query, spatial data display, simple spatial analysis, data in GIS, GIS capabilities, GIS data structures and sources of data, GIS tools, GIS analysis, GIS applications and GIS visualization. Prerequisites: CVE 243 and senior standing.

CVE 478.d: Explores properties, design and applications of sustainable concretes and their use in innovative design solutions. Covers design of green concrete mixes based on current codes and specifications with emphasis on carbon emission reduction. Evaluates the properties of sustainable concrete and its use in concrete production. Employs the application of advanced materials and methods in design of sustainable concrete. Applies LEED and Estidama ratings for green buildings. Uses software to evaluate service life and cost of sustainable concrete. Prerequisites: CVE 202 and CVE 224.

CVE 490.d: Covers the engineering design process through an open-ended, teambased project of disciplinary relevance. Applies discipline-specific methods and tools to problem identification, definition of objectives and constraints, evaluation of alternatives, and development of a preliminary design. Addresses factors such as sustainability, safety, ethics, economics, societal impact and standards in the design process. Emphasizes the aspects of innovation, entrepreneurship and intellectual property. Develops professional teamwork and communication skills. Prerequisites: ENG 204 and senior standing; prerequisite/concurrent: IEN 301.

CVE 491.d: Continues the work of CVE 490. Emphasizes the application of engineering principles to solve real-world problems. Includes exposure to industry practices through interaction with companies or professionals. Prerequisite: CVE 490.

CVE 497.d: Provides opportunities for the application of engineering knowledge and skills to actual problems in a real-life work setting. Enhances learning and soft skills through practical experience. Reinforces objectivesetting and performance measurement through a structured reporting process. Requires a minimum of 16 weeks of approved professional experience of onthe-job training. Graded as Pass/No pass. Prerequisites: ENG 204, junior standing and approval of internship coordinator. EGM Engineering Management

EGM 361.d: Focuses on engineers as managers. Includes the following topics: nature and functions of organizations; the tools of engineering management; engineering organizational models, including cluster and matrix organization; leadership; teamwork and creativity; personnel management; finance; communication skills; and ethical and professional standards. Introduces total quality management. Includes case studies. Prerequisite: sophomore II standing.

EGM 362.d: Covers projects in engineering organizations. Includes the following topics: project initiation; effective project management; project life cycle, planning and scheduling; resourcing; cost estimating; and project monitoring and control. Introduces computer packages. Includes case studies. Prerequisite: sophomore II standing.

EGM 363.d: Introduces the principles and practices of cost and value analysis and engineering. Emphasizes methods and tools on product and process cost estimation and reduction. Presents the value methodology process as an organizational creative approach and an effective tool for problem solving, quality assurance and operational excellence. Covers value concept, change management, thinking methodologies, risk management and phases of value engineering. Prerequisite: IEN 301.

EGM 364.d: Explores the economics concepts and theories of planning. Covers the bases and methods of economic analysis of engineering projects and the application of these principles in understanding economic activity of private and public engineering companies at various microand macroeconomic levels. Not open to civil engineering students. Prerequisite: sophomore II standing. ELE Electrical Engineering

ELE 101.d: Provides an overview of the electrical engineering fields and profession. Discusses contemporary and emerging applications and trends. Examines elementary concepts of electric circuits. Explores design of electrical systems. Includes teamwork skills through Undergraduate Course Descriptions a hands-on project.

ELE 211.d: Examines physical concepts and mathematical analysis of electric circuits. Includes DC, transient and sinusoidal steady state circuit analysis. Covers single phase AC power analysis. Includes laboratory experiments and use of modern software tools. Prerequisites: PHY 102 and PHY 102L.

ELE 212.d: Covers magnetically coupled inductors and ideal transformers, frequency response analysis, Laplace transform, application of Laplace transform in circuit analysis, two port networks. Introduces three phase circuits. Includes laboratory experiments. Prerequisites: ELE 211 or ELE 225, and MTH 205 or MTH 225.

ELE 225.d: Covers electrical quantities and variables; circuit principles; signal processing circuits; DC and AC circuit analysis; and diodes, transistors, operational amplifiers and digital devices. Not open to electrical engineering or computer engineering students. Prerequisites: PHY 102 and PHY 102L.

ELE 241.d: Reviews semiconductor physics. Covers PN junction, diode circuits, special diodes, BJT transistors, MOSFET transistors, transistor biasing, small signal analysis and design of MOSFET amplifiers, and digital electronics. Prerequisite: ELE 211.

ELE 311.d: Addresses vector algebra and vector calculus. Covers topics related to electrostatic and magnetostatic fields, electric and magnetic properties of media, electric boundary value problems, Maxwell’s equations, electromagnetic waves and plane wave propagation, Poynting theorem and transmission line theory. Prerequisites: MTH 203, MTH 205 or MTH 225, PHY 102 and PHY 102L.

ELE 320.d: Examines concepts of linear systems and signals and their applications to communications. Covers LTI systems, spectral-domain analysis, Z-transform and digital filters, analog-to-digital conversion, baseband and bandpass communications systems, signal transmission and impairments, and transmission media and link design. Not open to electrical engineering students. Prerequisites: ELE 211 and MTH 205.

ELE 321.d: Covers classification and manipulation of continuous-time and discrete-time signals, linear time invariant system modeling, convolution of discrete-time and continuous signals, Fourier representation of signals (Fourier series, Fourier transform and discrete-time Fourier transform), applications of Fourier representations in signals and systems, and the Z-transform and analysis of discrete-time systems. Prerequisite: ELE 212.

ELE 324.d: Covers treatment of sampling/reconstruction, quantization, discrete-time signals and systems, digital filtering, Z-transforms, transfer functions, digital filter realizations, discrete Fourier transform (DFT) and fast Fourier transform (FFT), finite impulse response (FIR) and infinite impulse response (IIR) filter design, and digital signal processing (DSP) applications. Prerequisite: ELE 321.

ELE 332L.d: Includes error analysis, linear displacement transducers, strain gauge, rotational speed measurement, capacitive and inductive transducers, temperature measurement, measurement of pressure and flow, and ultrasonic measurement systems. Prerequisite: ELE 341.

ELE 241L.d: Laboratory to accompany ELE 241. Not open to electrical engineering students. Prerequisite/concurrent: ELE 241.

ELE 340.d: Covers operational amplifiers and their applications, Darlington Pair amplifiers, data conversion circuits, timing and clock circuits, CMOS logic gates and semiconductor memory. Introduces BiCMOS technology. Not open to electrical engineering students. Prerequisites: ELE 241 and COE 221.

ELE 341.d: Covers differential pair, operational amplifiers, power amplifiers, frequency response characteristics of amplifiers, feedback and stability, active filters, digital to analog conversion (D/A) and analog to digital conversion (A/D) circuits. Prerequisite: ELE 241; prerequisite/concurrent: ELE 342L.

ELE 342L.d: Introduces electronic printed circuit board manufacturing, assembly and testing. Covers the design and testing of amplifiers, differential pair circuits, operational amplifier systems and mixed signals circuits. Prerequisite/concurrent: ELE 341 or ISM 243.

ELE 352.d: Covers magnetic circuits, single phase transformer and equivalent circuit, autotransformer, basic concepts of electromechanical energy conversion, and DC and AC machines modeling and steady-state analysis. Prerequisite: ELE 212.

ELE 353.d: (Equivalent to MCE 410). Examines mathematical models of systems, feedback control system characteristics, transient response analysis, performance and stability of feedback control systems, root locus analysis, frequency response analysis and design of feedback control systems. Prerequisite: ELE 212 or ISM 361.

ELE 353L.d: Laboratory to accompany ELE 353. Prerequisite: ELE 353.

ELE 360.d: Covers concepts of probability theory, random variables, stochastic processes and queuing systems emphasizing their applications in electrical engineering. Investigates electrical engineering systems and applications as well as networks performance via discreteevent simulation. Not open to students who have completed COE 375. Prerequisites: NGN 211 or STA 201, and ELE 320 or MTH 312 or prerequisite/concurrent: ELE 321 or ISM 351.

ELE 361.d: Covers signals and systems concepts, communication systems and signal transmission through linear systems; continuous wave modulation schemes including amplitude modulation (AM), frequency modulation (FM) and phase modulation (PM); detection schemes for analog modulation systems and superheterodyne receivers; and noise modeling and performance of various analog modulation schemes in the presence of noise. Includes fundamentals of digital communications. Prerequisite: ELE 321 or ELE 320; prerequisite/concurrent: ELE 360.

ELE 361L.d: Laboratory to accompany ELE 361. Prerequisite: ELE 361.

ELE 371.d: Examines power system concepts and per unit quantities; transmission line, transformer and rotating machine modeling; steady-state analysis and power flow; balanced fault analysis; theory of symmetrical components; and unbalanced fault analysis. Prerequisite: ELE 352.

ELE 372L.d: Laboratory to accompany ELE 371. Prerequisite/concurrent: ELE 371.

ELE 432.d: (Equivalent to BME 420). Examines principles of medical instrumentation. Covers biomedical sensors and transducers; temperature, displacement, acoustical, chemical and radiation measurements; bio-potential amplifiers and signal processing; origin of biopotentials; bio-potential electrodes; measurement of bio-potentials such as ECG, EEG and EMG; blood pressure measurements; and electrical safety. Prerequisite: ELE 341 or ISM 243.

ELE 440.d: Covers transmitter and receiver architectures, link budget, noise analysis, linearity analysis, case study (transmitter/ receiver design), linear amplifier design, network analysis, microwave measurements for transmitters’ characterization, EDA tools with application to system level design and analysis. Prerequisite: ISM 243 or prerequisite/concurrent: ELE 341.

ELE 441.d: Covers conceptual and functional description of the physics, characteristics and fabrication of microelectronic devices as it applies to current and future integrated circuits (IC) and systems. Includes properties and dynamics of semiconductor carriers, P-N junctions, MOSFETs, BJTs and modern FETs. Uses of the state-of-the-art technology CAD/CAE simulation tools, analytical techniques for device design, layout, fabrication and testing. Prerequisite: ELE 341.

ELE 444.d: Covers state-space modeling and analysis, controllability, observability, state feedback design and pole placement, dynamic observers, output feedback design and stability analysis. Prerequisite: ELE 353 or MCE 410.

ELE 451.d: Provides an overview of wireless networks, design considerations of cellular systems, frequency reuse, multiple access interference, wireless channel characterization, Rayleigh fading, shadowing, modulation techniques for mobile radio, diversity schemes, multiple access techniques, wireless systems and standards. Prerequisite: ELE 361.

ELE 452.d: Covers model of digital communication systems, base-band transmission and line coding techniques, geometric interpretation of signals, band-pass transmission and digital modulation techniques, optimum detection of known signals in AWGN channels, error correcting codes, and modulation and coding tradeoff. Prerequisite: ELE 361.

ELE 453.d: Examines electromagnetic plane waves, microwave transmission lines, Smith charts and stubs, microwave waveguides and components, microwave measurements and applications, and microwave generators. Prerequisite: ELE 311. Undergraduate Course Descriptions

ELE 454.d: Covers radiation pattern, directivity and gain, half-power beam width and beam efficiency, antenna bandwidth, polarization, input impedance, radiation efficiency, wire antennas, loop antennas, array antennas, aperture antennas and reflector antennas. Prerequisite: ELE 311.

ELE 456.d: Covers fundamentals of pattern recognition. Explores the following topics: Bayesian decision theory and parameter estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, linear discriminant analysis, Fisher discriminant analysis, dimensionality reduction via principal component analysis, and neural networks. Includes unsupervised learning and clustering. Prerequisites: CMP 120 or NGN 112, and MTH 221 or MTH 225; prerequisite/concurrent: ELE 360.

ELE 457.d: Focuses on satellite communications. Covers Kepler’s laws of orbital motion, satellite’s look angles calculations, satellite subsystems and transponders classification, satellite antennas, link budget analysis, multiple access techniques and modulation. Prerequisite: ELE 311; prerequisite/concurrent: ELE 361.

ELE 458.d: Provides an overview of multimedia information (text, video, audio and images). Explains the fundamentals of image and video compression. Introduces underlying concepts and principles of multimedia technologies and networking. Demonstrates basic understanding of Quality of Service (QoS) and QoS Routing network protocols, routing, operating systems and human computer interaction. Includes multimedia streaming standards and techniques over wired and wireless networks. Prerequisite/concurrent: ELE 360 or COE 375.

ELE 459.d: Focuses on radar systems and their applications. Includes the following topics: the radar range equation, detection fundamentals, the radar cross-section, antennas, radar transmitters and receivers, pulse Doppler radars, moving target indictors, tracking radars and synthetic aperture radars. Prerequisite: ELE 311.

ELE 460.d: Explores the following topics: basics of machine learning, neural networks and their programming tools, deep convolutional neural networks, autoencoders, denoising autoecoders, variational autoencoders, recurrent networks, LSTM networks, practical issues in training deep networks and examples of very deep networks. Involves project based practical learning, and hence practical training in the subject. Prerequisites: NGN 112, NGN 211, and MTH 221 or MTH 225.

ELE 470.d: Covers mobile robot locomotion, kinematics, perception, localization, pathplanning and navigation. Introduces robot swarm concepts, quadcopter drone dynamics and Robot Operating System (ROS) concepts. Prerequisite: ELE 353 or MCE 410.

ELE 471.d: Covers discrete-time system models, open loop and closed-loop discrete-time systems, time-response characteristics, stability analysis techniques, digital controller design and implementation techniques, state-space representations of discrete-time systems, state-feedback and pole-placement design. Prerequisites: ELE 321 or ISM 351, and ELE 353 or MCE 410.

ELE 481.d: Covers unsymmetrical fault analysis, fuses, voltage and current transducers, fundamental relay operating principles and characteristics, over current protection, comparators and static relay circuits, differential protection and its application to generators, transformers and bus bars, motor protection, system grounding, standard protective schemes for system coordination of relays. Prerequisite: ELE 371.

ELE 482.d: Examines concepts and techniques associated with the design and operation of electrical distribution systems. Includes the following topics: load characteristics, distribution substations, choice of voltage levels, loss minimization and voltage control, calculation of impedances of unbalanced three-phase systems, and analysis techniques of radial systems. Prerequisite: ELE 371.

ELE 483.d: Examines concepts, design aspects and control techniques associated with the utilization of electrical energy in different fields. Includes the following topics: laws of illumination, operating concepts of different lamps, identification of lighting requirements, design of lighting layouts, design of residential wiring including photovoltaic systems, analysis and calculations of electric drive systems, and operation of electric vehicles and traction systems. Prerequisite: ELE 352.

ELE 485.d: Covers operating characteristics of power semiconductor devices such as bipolar junction transistors (BJTs), insulated gate bipolar transistors (IGBTs), metal-oxide semiconductor field-effect transistors (MOSFETs) and Thyristors. Covers the fundamentals of power converter circuits including dc/dc converters, phase controlled ac/dc rectifiers and dc/ac inverters. Addresses practical issues in the Undergraduate Course Descriptions design and implementation of power converters. Prerequisites: ELE 212 and ELE 241.

ELE 486.d: Covers the application of semiconductor switching power converters to adjustable speed DC and AC motor drives. Includes the following topics: steady state theory and analysis of electric motion control in industrial, robotic and traction systems. Prerequisites: ELE 241 and ELE 352.

ELE 487.d: Covers renewable energy conversion systems. Introduces modeling and control of renewable energy sources such as wind and solar energy systems. Addresses power electronics topologies and interfaces for renewable energy systems. Covers integration of renewable energy systems with the distribution grid. Prerequisite: ELE 352.

ELE 490.d: Covers the engineering design process through an open-ended, team-based project of disciplinary relevance. Applies discipline-specific methods and tools to problem identification, definition of objectives and constraints, evaluation of alternatives, and development of a preliminary design. Addresses factors such as sustainability, safety, ethics, economics, societal impact and standards in the design process. Emphasizes the aspects of innovation, entrepreneurship and intellectual property. Develops professional teamwork and communication skills. Prerequisites: ENG 204, senior standing and permission of the department; prerequisites/concurrent: IEN 301 and COE 242.

ELE 491.d: Continues the work of ELE 490. Emphasizes the application of engineering principles to solve real-world problems. Includes exposure to industry practices through interaction with companies or professionals. Prerequisite: ELE 490. EWE Environmental and Water Engineering

ELE 497.d: Provides opportunities for the application of engineering knowledge and skills to actual problems in a real-life work setting. Enhances learning and soft skills through practical experience. Reinforces objectivesetting and performance measurement through a structured reporting process. Requires a minimum of 16 weeks of approved professional experience of onthe-job training. Graded as Pass/No Pass. Prerequisites: ENG 204, junior standing and approval of internship coordinator.

EWE 331.d: Introduces different components of water resources engineering and environmental engineering, environmental sustainability, environmental and social impact assessment, and environmental risk assessment. Covers surface and groundwater hydrology, quantity and quality of water resources, water supply systems and pollution originating from air, noise and solid waste. Prerequisites: CHM 101 and CHM 101L.

EWE 333.d: Introduces water quality criteria, standards, water sampling and testing methods. Covers pollution sources in water bodies and their impacts on aquatic life. Covers water demand, forecasting and waste generation, and provides a guide to selecting water and wastewater treatment processes. Introduces resource recovery options from water and wastewater treatment facilities. Introduces water reuse options, the importance of pretreatment and quality requirements. Prerequisites: CHM 101 and CHM 101L. INE Industrial Engineering

INE 202.d: Presents a broad introduction to the principles and practices of industrial engineering. Discusses industrial engineering concepts to design and operate manufacturing and service systems. Provides a basic understanding of industrial engineering decisions and analytical tools. Develops an appreciation of how the applications of industrial engineering concepts and tools provide competitive advantages for organizations across industries. Prerequisite: NGN 110.

INE 222.d: Introduces deterministic models in operations research with special emphasis on linear programming. Covers simplex method, duality, sensitivity analysis, transportation and assignment problems, shortest path problem, CPM/PERT, maximum flow problem, and minimum spanning tree problem. Provides real modeling of various industrial problems as linear programs. Prerequisite: INE 202; prerequisite/concurrent: MTH 225.

INE 302.d: Provides the fundamentals of the economical manufacturing of products. Encompasses many manufacturing processes for different materials including metals, metal powders, ceramics, polymers and composites. Covers different manufacturing processes including material removal, casting, bulk deformation and assembly. Introduces contemporary topics such as additive and nano-manufacturing. Prerequisites: INE 216L or MCE 216L; and MCE 230; prerequisites/concurrent: INE 302L.

INE 302L.d: Provides hands-on experience in metrology, different machining operations, numerically controlled machining, casting, additive manufacturing, bulk and sheet metal forming, powder metallurgy, processing of polymers and composites, and assembly and joining operations. Prerequisite/concurrent: INE 302.

INE 310.d: Covers the development of data and information systems solutions for engineering problems including data models, database development and SQL. Introduces data modeling, summarization and visualization in spreadsheets and business intelligence tools. Covers forecasting and predictive models through spreadsheet tools. Prerequisites: INE 202, and NGN 211 or STA 201.

INE 311.d: Emphasizes the importance of quality management and control. Deals with statistical methods relevant to process control, control charts for variables and attributes, process capability analysis and acceptance sampling plans. Introduces process improvement techniques and six sigma concepts and their applications. Prerequisite: NGN 211 or STA 201.

INE 322.d: Covers deterministic models in operations research and their solution methods. Introduces integer programming formulation and branch and bound method, deterministic dynamic programming, nonlinear programming formulation and unconstrained and constrained optimization techniques. Provides real applications of integer, dynamic and nonlinear programs to industrial and engineering problems. Prerequisite: INE 222; prerequisite/concurrent: MTH 203.

INE 323.d: Introduces stochastic processes and simulation modeling and techniques. Covers discrete and continuous Markov chains, Poisson processes, renewal reward processes, discrete event simulation, simulation languages, model verification and validation. Discusses applications to queuing, reliability and inventory systems. Prerequisites: INE 202, and NGN 211 or STA 201.

INE 331.d: Covers design and analysis of production systems. Introduces the managerial concepts and quantitative techniques required in production planning and inventory control. Includes aggregate production planning, master production scheduling, material requirement planning, single and multiple products inventory control in both certain and uncertain environments. Prerequisites: INE 222, and NGN 211 or STA 201.

INE 332.d: Presents various concepts, tools and techniques of supply chain management (SCM). Deals with development and application of supply chain decision models with special emphasis on supply network design, supply chain performance metrics, inventory, transportation, sustainability, supply chain risk management and digital transformation. Explores various SCM initiatives that enhance supply chain collaboration. Prerequisite: INE 331; prerequisite/concurrent: INE 322.

INE 333.d: Deals with principles and practices of facility design and planning and materials handling equipment for manufacturing and service systems. Includes analytical approaches in site location, facility design and layout, materials handling and storage systems. Emphasizes quantitative methods for warehouse layout and facility location theory. Prerequisite: INE 331. Undergraduate Course Descriptions

INE 413.d: Covers maintenance workload analysis and calculations, capacity planning of maintenance resources, maintenance work scheduling, maintenance auditing and the measurement of maintenance operations performance, and computerized maintenance management systems (CMMS). Explores recent maintenance concepts and techniques such as predictive maintenance and enterprise asset management. Prerequisites: INE 322 and INE 323. procedures to solve such problems. Prerequisite: INE 332.

INE 415.d: Introduces the planning, design and statistical analysis of experiments. Includes analysis of variance (ANOVA), randomized block design, factorial and fractional design, random and mixed models, and response surface methods. Stresses the application of the learned techniques to various engineering problems. Prerequisite: INE 311.

INE 416.d: Covers the concepts of reliability and failure analysis. Addresses hazard and reliability functions, reliability data analysis and reliability modeling. Explores recent reliability concepts and techniques such as reliability-centered maintenance. Prerequisite: INE 323.

INE 417.d: Covers the concepts of Six Sigma methodology for both manufacturing and service organizations. Introduces lean, six sigma and the DMAIC problem-solving methodology. Discusses continuous process improvement techniques such as process definition, process flow diagrams, data collection, measurement techniques, causes of process variation, Pareto diagrams, cause and effect diagrams, and statistical-based techniques. Prerequisite: INE 311.

INE 418.d: Introduces the concepts and methods of decision science. Integrates the application of operations research, analytics methods/techniques and design thinking to real-world decision problems. Explores model-based analyses of complex situations in both service and manufacturing sectors through a disciplined thinking process. Emphasizes applications of decision science in areas such as supply chain management, healthcare, customer service and manufacturing systems. Prerequisites: INE 310 and INE 332.

INE 425.d: Introduces judgment and decision making of individuals, groups and organizations. Includes structured decision problems, decision trees, Bayesian decision analysis, utility theory and multi-criteria decision making. Covers practical applications from various engineering areas. Prerequisite: INE 323.

INE 431.d: Examines scheduling applications in manufacturing and services. Covers practical scheduling problems such as single machine, parallel machines, flow shop, job shop and project scheduling with unconstrained and constrained resources. Discuses both exact and approximate

INE 433.d: Provides an overview of transportation activities related to design, evaluation and performance of logistics systems. Covers the physical and information flows in supply chains and the economic drivers of logistic choices. Addresses methods to analyze and improve logistics and transportation systems, technology and infrastructure. Prerequisite: INE 332.

INE 439.d: Covers fundamentals and basic principles associated with manufacturing systems and their automation. Discusses quantitative models and metrics to describe and compare production performance in various types of manned and automated systems. Includes manned and automated single station, assembly and production lines; group and flexible manufacturing systems; material handling systems; process planning and control; and lean and sustainable manufacturing. Prerequisites: INE 302 and INE 302L.

INE 450.d: Introduces safety regulations and standards, industrial hazard avoidance concepts and techniques, and plant safety applications. Covers process safety, analytical trees and fault tree analysis, risk assessment, and emergency planning. Prerequisite: senior standing.

INE 460.d: Provides an overview of Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems. Focuses on how production and related processes interact in an integrated environment. Covers financial and management accounting, purchase-to-pay, plan-to-produce, order-to-cash, and enterprise asset management. Discusses case studies and real-life applications. Not open to students who have completed MGT 315. Prerequisite: INE 331 and EGM 364.

INE 465.d: Examines models of reducing costs, increasing revenue and enhancing customer service in service industries. Covers the management of service systems, analysis of service systems using operations management and operations research (OM/OR) techniques, evaluation of the performance of service systems, Undergraduate Course Descriptions service thinking and service industry applications. Prerequisite/concurrent: INE 332.

INE 490.d: Covers the engineering design process through an open-ended, team-based project of disciplinary relevance. Applies discipline-specific methods and tools to problem identification, definition of objectives and constraints, evaluation of alternatives, and development of a preliminary design. Addresses factors such as sustainability, safety, ethics, economics, societal impact and standards in the design process. Emphasizes the aspects of innovation, entrepreneurship and intellectual property. Develops professional teamwork and communication skills. Prerequisite: ENG 204; prerequisites/concurrent: IEN 301, INE 311 and INE 332.

INE 491.d: Continues the work of INE 490. Emphasizes the application of engineering principles to solve real-world problems. Includes exposure to industry practices through interaction with companies or professionals. Prerequisite: INE 490.

INE 497.d: Provides opportunities for the application of engineering knowledge and skills to actual problems in a real-life work setting. Enhances learning and soft skills through practical experience. Reinforces objectivesetting and performance measurement through a structured reporting process. Requires a minimum of 16 weeks of approved professional experience of onthe-job training. Graded as Pass/No Pass. Prerequisites: ENG 204, junior standing and approval of internship coordinator. ISM Intelligent Systems and Mechatronics Engineering

ISM 210.d: Covers number systems and information representation. Introduces Boolean algebra, design of combinational and sequential logic circuits. Examines basic building blocks, addressing modes, instruction sets for microcontrollers and microprocessors. Covers microcontroller programming and interfacing for analog/digital input/output, timers and interrupts. Introduces serial communication concepts and evaluates application dependent selection criteria for microcontrollers. Prerequisite: ISM 216L or MCE 226L.

ISM 231.d: Covers the basic concepts of thermodynamics, properties of matter, processes and cycles, energy transfer and first law of thermodynamics. Covers properties of fluids, kinematics of fluid motion, conservation of mass, Bernoulli’s equation, conservation of momentum and head losses in pipes. Introduces the different mechanisms of heat transfer. Prerequisite: MCE 224.

ISM 243.d: Covers diode circuits; MOSFET transistor; biasing, small signal analysis and design of MOSFET amplifiers; operational amplifiers; power amplifiers; frequency response characteristics of amplifiers; active filters; digital electronics; and digital to analog conversion (D/A) and analog to digital conversion (A/D). Prerequisite: ELE 211.

ISM 351.d: Covers signal classification and system behavior, impulse response and convolution, signals and systems analysis and representation via the Fourier transform and the ztransform, digital filter design, and application of basic machine learning methods. Prerequisites: ELE 211 and MTH 225.

ISM 361.d: Introduces the concept and application of mechanical, electrical systems and instrumentations for mechatronics system integration. Covers theoretical modeling and analysis of translational and rotational mechanical systems, electrical systems, and electromechanical systems, Laplace transforms, transfer functions, forced and free response, state space model representation, measurement systems and transducers, sensors and signal conditioning, and actuators. Prerequisites: MCE 224 and MTH 225; prerequisites/concurrent: ISM 243; and ISM 316L or MCE 326L.

ISM 364L.d: Covers the fundamental concepts of measurement and signal acquisition, system dynamics, and control systems through theory and experimentation, including converting physical phenomena to a measurable signal; conditioning, acquiring and analyzing the signal; studying dynamic systems’ response in the time and frequency domains; and open loop and closed loop control of various mechatronics systems. Uses CAD software for dynamic response and controller design. Prerequisites: ISM 231, and ELE 353 or MCE 410.

ISM 371.d: Covers the application of semiconductor switching power converters to adjustable speed DC and AC motor drives. Includes the following topics: steady state theory and analysis of electric motion control in industrial, robotic and traction systems. Prerequisite: ISM 243.

ISM 382.d: Covers connectivity aspects in Internet of Things systems; protocol stacks; the radio layer including channel impairments, errors and link budget; the modem layer including modulation, synchronization and spread spectrum communications; the medium access control layer including multiple access and error detection and correction. Includes an overview of wireless standards for IoT. Prerequisite: ISM 351; prerequisite/concurrent: ELE 360.

ISM 383.d: Covers many models and algorithms used in making machines intelligent with focus on the applications of these algorithms on time domain, spatial domain, and frequency domain representations of signals, extracted from audio, video or other sensory inputs. Discusses how to combine information from multiple modalities. Algorithms discussed include linear and non-linear multivariate models, multi-layer neural networks, ensemble methods, Markov decision processes, unsupervised learning, and reinforcement learning. Prerequisites: ISM 351, and ISM 216L or MCE 226L; prerequisite/concurrent: ELE 360.

ISM 391L.d: Covers applications of theoretical principles in mechanical, electrical and computer knowledge incorporating sensors, actuators and intelligence for mechatronics systems. Develops an intelligent mechatronic system, including a microcontroller interfacing with powerelectronics components, sensors and actuators. Explores industrial mechatronic systems such as programmable logic controllers. Prerequisite: ISM 364L.

ISM 411.d: Covers basic human neurophysiology, human senses, electroencephalograph signal recording, EEG signal acquisition, preprocessing and machine learning. Covers brain computer interface applications such as prosthetic devices, nerve stimulation, cognitive enhancement and ethics in brain computer interface. Prerequisites: ISM 243 and ISM 351.

ISM 412.d: Covers stochastic signal models and the Yule-Walker equations, minimum variance and maximum likelihood estimation, non-parametric and parametric spectral estimation, optimum and adaptive FIR filtering. Introduces array processing techniques such as direction of arrival estimation and adaptive beamforming. Prerequisites: ELE 360, ISM 351 and MTH 225.

ISM 431.d: Covers hydraulic and pneumatic systems and their use to transfer and control power. Analyzes various aspects of fluid power, fluid mechanics, governing laws, pumps and motors, cavitation, and noise. Covers fundamentals and specific cases of control valves such as direction, pressure and flow control with emphasis on actuators, and servo and electrohydraulic valves. Prerequisite: ISM 231 or MCE 240.

ISM 442.d: Introduces concepts of automotive electronics, solid state sensors and actuators, onboard electronic safety systems, electronic control systems in automotives, communications and radar protocols in automotives, navigation and GPS systems, cruise control systems, modern electronic display panels, digital transformation in cars and airplanes. Prerequisite: ELE 341 or ISM 243. Undergraduate Course Descriptions electrostatic, thermal, piezoresistive, piezoelectric and magnetic. Prerequisite: ISM 361 or MCE 313.

ISM 443.d: Covers concepts related to the design, modeling, materials and applications of MEMS. Discusses fundamental microfabrication methods using silicon wafers. Includes basic elements of solid mechanics, mechanical vibrations and response characteristics of transducers pertaining to the development of MEMS sensors and actuators. Examines several transduction principles commonly used in MEMS sensors and actuators, including

ISM 484.d: Examines the smart grids concept, power system concepts and per unit quantities; steadystate analysis and power flow; and demand response, optimal power flow, renewable energy resources, and their integration with the smart grids. Prerequisites: ISM 371 and MTH 225.

ISM 490.d: Covers the engineering design process through an open-ended, team-based project of disciplinary relevance. Applies disciplinespecific methods and tools to problem identification, definition of objectives and constraints, evaluation of alternatives, and development of a preliminary design. Addresses factors such as sustainability, safety, ethics, economics, societal impact and standards in the design process. Emphasizes the aspects of innovation, entrepreneurship and intellectual property. Develops professional teamwork and communication skills. Prerequisites: senior standing, ENG 204, ISM 210, MCE 223 and MCE 236L; prerequisites/concurrent: IEN 301 and ISM 383.

ISM 433.d: Provides students with a comprehensive understanding of the principles, technologies and applications of intelligent manufacturing systems. Covers an introduction to conventional manufacturing and computer-aided manufacturing; automation and robotics; data analytics, artificial intelligence and the Internet of Things (IoT) in manufacturing; sustainable manufacturing; and Industry 4.0. Provides students with the necessary skills to design, analyze and optimize intelligent manufacturing systems for improved efficiency, productivity and quality. Prerequisites: NGN 112, and ISM 316L or MCE 326L.

ISM 491.d: Continues the work of ISM 490. Emphasizes the application of engineering principles to solve real-world problems. Includes exposure to industry practices through interaction with companies or professionals. Prerequisite: ISM 490.

ISM 497.d: Provides opportunities for the application of engineering knowledge and skills to actual problems in a real-life work setting. Enhances learning and soft skills through practical experience. Reinforces objectivesetting and performance measurement through a structured reporting process. Requires a minimum of 16 weeks of approved professional experience of fulltime on-the-job training. Graded as Pass/No Pass. Prerequisites: junior II standing and approval of internship coordinator. MCE Mechanical Engineering

MCE 216L.d: Covers descriptive geometry, orthographic projections, and computer-aided drafting using commercial computer-aided design software. Introduces the use of basic machines, the development of hand skills and safety in the workshop. Covers basic hand tools, basic machining operations, welding, casting, woodwork, sheet metal work and measuring instruments. Not open to students who have completed INE 216L.

MCE 220.d: Covers fundamental concepts and principles of mechanics, vectors and force systems. Topics include concepts of free-bodydiagram; principles of equilibrium of particles and rigid bodies in two and three dimensions; analysis of structures: trusses, frames and machines; shear and bending moment in beams; center of gravity; centroids; area moment of inertia; and friction. Not open to civil engineering students. Prerequisites: PHY 101 and PHY 101L.

MCE 222.d: Examines fundamental concepts of kinematics and kinetics with application to motion of particles and plane motion of rigid bodies. Includes the following topics: rectilinear and curvilinear motion of particles; Newton’s second law, impulse and momentum methods; impact, dynamics of systems of particles; kinematics of rigid bodies; plane motion of rigid bodies; forces and accelerations; and energy and momentum methods. Prerequisites: MCE 220 and MTH 104.

MCE 223.d: (Equivalent to CVE 223). Covers stress and strain; mechanical properties of materials; axial load, torsion, bending and transverse shear; combined loadings; stress transformation; deflection of beams and shafts; and buckling of columns. Prerequisite: MCE 220 or MCE 224.

MCE 224.d: Covers statics of particles and rigid bodies, vector mechanics, free body diagrams, two-andthree-dimensional force equilibrium systems, truss structures and frames, friction, centroid and moment of inertia, dynamics of particles in rectilinear and curvilinear motions, Newton’s second law, considerations of work and energy, and kinematics of rigid bodies. Not open to mechanical engineering or civil engineering students. Prerequisites: MTH 104, PHY 101 and PHY 101L.

MCE 310.d: Covers modeling and analysis of translational and rotational mechanical systems, electrical systems and electromechanical systems; system time response and Laplace transform techniques; basic concepts of state-space and input/ output systems representation; operating principles of electromechanical systems and DC/AC actuators. Prerequisites: PHY 102 and MCE 222; prerequisite/concurrent: MCE 326L.

MCE 226L.d: (Equivalent to ISM 216L). Covers Boolean algebra, numbering systems, basic computer hardware, C-programming with focus on input-output, logic statements, loops, arrays, pointers and computer interfacing.

MCE 230.d: Introduces material science; relationships between structure and properties of materials; atomic bonding, crystalline structures, crystal defects and imperfections; phase diagrams and equilibrium; microstructural development; properties of engineering materials; and corrosion. Prerequisites: CHM 101 and CHM 101L. Undergraduate Course Descriptions

MCE 236L.d: Covers dimensioning, an introduction to fits and tolerances, detailed and assembly drawings, solid modeling and computeraided drafting using commercial computer-aided design software. Prerequisite: MCE 216L.

MCE 240.d: Covers fundamental concepts and properties of fluids; fluid statics, forces on planar and curved surfaces, and buoyancy; kinematics of fluid motion; conservation equations with applications; continuity, momentum and energy equations, and Bernoulli’s equation; velocity and flow rate measurements; dimensional analysis and similitude; and head losses in pipes. Prerequisites: MCE 220 or MCE 224, and MTH 104.

MCE 241.d: (Equivalent to CHE 214). Covers basic concepts of thermodynamics, properties of matter, processes and cycles, energy transfer, first law of thermodynamics for closed systems and control volumes, second law of thermodynamics, introduction to cycle analysis, entropy and exergy analyses and engineering applications. Not open to chemical engineering students. Prerequisites: PHY 101 and PHY 101L.

MCE 313.d: Covers basic concepts of measuring methods; elements of electrical circuits; static and dynamic characteristics of signals; types of errors; sampling; signal conditioning; data acquisition; physical aspects of temperature, pressure, fluid flow, force, stress, strain and torque measurements; assessing and presenting measured data; and uncertainty analysis. Covers dynamic response of measurement systems and computer simulations. Prerequisites: MCE 222; prerequisite/concurrent: MCE 310.

MCE 313L.d: Covers fundamental concepts of measurement and signal acquisition through theory and experimentation, including transduction mechanisms of physical phenomena, signal acquisition, conditioning and analysis. Includes laboratory experiments with emphasis on electrical circuits and signal conditioners along with pressure, temperature, motion and strain measurements. Prerequisite/concurrent: MCE 313.

MCE 323.d: Covers the process of materials selection, stress, strain, and deflection of solid elements as applied to mechanical design. Covers failure prevention under static and fatigue loading conditions in addition to the design and selection of mechanical elements including power screws, bearings, gears, and shafts. Prerequisites: MCE 223; prerequisite/concurrent: MCE 331.

MCE 325.d: (Equivalent to CVE 325). Covers basic concepts of computational methods; error analysis; numerical solutions of linear and nonlinear algebraic equations; numerical approximations: regression and interpolation; numerical differentiation and integration; numerical solution of ordinary differential equations: initial and boundary value problems, eigenvalue problems; introduction to numerical solution of partial differential equations; and engineering applications using software. Prerequisites: MCE 326L; and MTH 225, or both MTH 205 and MTH 221.

MCE 326L.d: (Equivalent to ISM 316L). Covers MATLAB programming software, input-output, loops functions, s-functions and embedded MATLAB functions. Introduces Simulink MATLAB toolbox for mechanical simulations. Includes a term project on interfacing a mechanical system to computer hardware. Prerequisite: MCE 226L.

MCE 331.d: Covers the fundamentals of manufacturing processes, including casting, forming, welding and machining operations. Introduces basics of economics of metal cutting, statistical quality control, non-metals manufacturing and other contemporary topics in manufacturing. Prerequisites: MCE 216L, MCE 220 or MCE 224, and MCE 230.

MCE 332L.d: Covers experimental determination of mechanical properties of engineering materials. Includes experiments covering different manufacturing processes such as casting, welding, forming and machining. Introduces new experiments on contemporary topics in materials and manufacturing. Prerequisite/concurrent: MCE 331.

MCE 341.d: Covers energy system analysis including modern power cycles, refrigeration and heat pump cycles; Maxwell relations and development of thermodynamic properties; thermodynamics of nonreacting and reacting mixtures of real and ideal gases; psychrometry and air conditioning processes; combustion fundamentals and chemical reactions. Prerequisite: MCE 241.

MCE 344.d: (Equivalent to CHE 307). Covers mechanisms of heat transfer, steady-state conduction in various geometries, electric network analogy, fins, numerical methods in heat transfer, transient conduction, natural and forced convection, internal and external heat transfer, heat exchanger analysis, and fundamentals of thermal radiation. Prerequisites: MCE 240 and MCE 241.

MCE 345L.d: Includes the experimental evaluation and analysis of the performance of energy systems, the thermal conductivity of solids and fluids, and the performance curves of pumps; and experiments on fluid flow, heat exchangers, cooling towers, internal combustion engines, and refrigeration and air conditioning systems. Prerequisites/concurrent: MCE 341 and MCE 344.

MCE 410.d: (Equivalent to ELE 353). Covers feedback system response, feedback control system characteristics, performance and stability of feedback control systems, root-locus techniques, frequency domain analysis and design of feedback control systems. Prerequisites: MCE 310 and MCE 313L; or ISM 361.

MCE 415L.d: Covers experiments on system dynamics, vibration and control systems. Includes experiments on dynamic systems’ response in the time and frequency domains, and open loop and closed loop control of various mechanical systems. Uses CAD software for dynamic response and controller design. Prerequisite/concurrent: MCE 410.

MCE 416.d: Explores kinematics and dynamic analysis and synthesis of linkages (displacement, velocity, acceleration and force analysis), camfollower, gear-train systems, and balancing of rotating systems. Prerequisite/concurrent: MCE 310 or ISM 361.

MCE 423.d: Provides a review of single and two degree-of-freedom vibration time and frequency response (free, transient and harmonic forcing). Includes analysis of multi-degree of freedom system (mass, stiffness and damping matrices). Covers modal analysis and frequency response functions (FRF), vibration analysis of continuous structures and finite element method. Covers vibration measurements and testing: vibration signal analysis, vibration isolation techniques, vibration measurements of active structures, including vibrating machines and rotating machinery. Prerequisite: MCE 310 or ISM 361.

MCE 438.d: Provides the skills needed to interpret codes and procedures in the fields of nondestructive testing (NDT). Covers NDT management and certification programs; basic principles of defect probability of detection (POD); surface inspection methods such as visual, penetrant and magnetic testing; and volumetric inspection methods such as ultrasonic and radiographic testing. Designs inspection techniques and analyzes inspection results. Prerequisites: MCE 313 and MCE 331.

MCE 445.d: Covers types of power plants, thermodynamics of power plants, combined power plants, systems components, design parameters, plant evaluation, efficiency calculations methods, modifications to improve system performance, cogeneration plants, thermodynamics and economics of cogeneration plants, system equipment, practical schemes of cogeneration plants, power plant economics, power plant planning, design concepts, power plant control, burner management and environmental impact of power plants. Prerequisites: MCE 341 and MCE 344.

MCE 446.d: Introduces ventilation, air conditioning and refrigeration; classification and selection of air conditioning systems; applied psychrometrics, design conditions, human thermal comfort and indoor air quality; heating and cooling loads calculations; vapor compression refrigeration cycles; refrigeration equipment and systems; heating equipment and systems; air distribution systems and duct design; and fire and smoke control in duct systems. Addresses American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers (ASHRAE). Covers software applications used to design conventional and nonconventional systems. Prerequisites: MCE 341 or CHE 304, and MCE 344.

MCE 451.d: Evaluates the effects of fossil fuels-based energy systems on the environment and society. Focuses on the fundamentals and main characteristics of renewable energy technologies such as solar (thermal and photovoltaic), hydropower, wind, geothermal, biomass, ocean thermal, wave and tidal energies. Addresses comparative environmental assessments between renewable energy systems and conventional fossil fuel systems. Focuses on the design of renewable/hybrid energy systems that are economically feasible, have a minimal impact on the environment and meet specific energy demands. Prerequisite: MCE 241.

MCE 452.d: Covers the basic concepts of fuel cells and fuel cell stacks. Discusses the design of various types of fuel cells such as phosphoric acid, alkaline, proton exchange membrane, molten carbonate, solid oxide and direct methanol fuel cells. Studies the technical aspects of fuel cells with respect to thermodynamics, transport phenomena and electrochemistry. Prerequisites: MCE 341 and MCE 344.

MCE 464.d: Gives an overview of robotics, robot coordinate systems, and direct and inverse kinematics. Introduces manipulator dynamics and force control and compliance. Includes robot sensors and control strategies, and requirement of digital control of robots. Prerequisite: MCE 310 or ELE 353 or ISM 361.

MCE 447.d: Covers fundamental principles of engine operation and applications, engine classifications, engine design and operating parameters, engine cycles, thermo-chemistry and fuels, air and fuel induction systems, fluid motion within combustion chambers, combustion in spark ignition engines, combustion in compression ignition engines, exhaust system, engine emission and air pollution, methods of emission control, engine friction and lubrication, and engine operating characteristics. Introduces Undergraduate Course Descriptions modeling of real engine flow and combustion processes, as well as new trends in internal combustion engines. Prerequisite: MCE 341.

MCE 466.d: Introduces the application of microprocessors and digital electronics to the design and application of control systems embedded in smart products. Covers sensors, actuators, software, system hardware and interfacing for mechanical engineering applications, as well as smart product design. Prerequisites: ELE 332L and ELE 353, or MCE 310 and prerequisite/concurrent MCE 313L.

MCE 450.d: Analyzes energy systems, including fossil fuels, steam, cogeneration, waste heat recovery, refrigeration and air conditioning systems; total energy management; energy management organization and approach; energy conservation in electrical load; lighting, building envelop, and insulation; economic energy analysis; energy auditing; monitoring and targeting; technical approaches and analyses; control; and energy management systems. Prerequisite: MCE 341.

MCE 473.d: Introduces Finite Element Method (FEM) and its application in different mechanical engineering problems. Includes theoretical and computational basics of finite element method, element formulation and assembly of global matrices. Uses commercial software to solve various engineering problems. Applications include solid mechanics, 2-D steady state heat conduction and fluid problems. Prerequisite: MCE 323; prerequisite/concurrent: MCE 344.

MCE 477.d: Examines advanced composite materials and applications. Covers stressstrain relationship for an orthotropic lamina, laminate analysis, static strength of laminates, analysis of laminated beams, introduction to micro-mechanical analysis of laminae, design applications and computer program applications. Prerequisites: MCE 230, and MTH 221 or MTH 225; prerequisite/concurrent: MCE 323.

MCE 482.d: Covers potential flow, stream function, velocity potential, plane flow past closed-body shapes, airfoil theory; fluid dynamic forces on immersed bodies, drag and lift, flow over cylinder, sphere and flat plate; fundamentals of compressible fluid flow, isentropic flow, shock waves and supersonic nozzles and friction and heat interaction; types of pumps and turbines, pumps and turbine scaling laws. Introduces the use of commercial computational fluid dynamics (CFD) software. Prerequisites/concurrent: MCE 325, MCE 345L and MTH 203.

MCE 485.d: Covers fundamentals of piping systems, hydraulic and mechanical design considerations, pipe sizing and selection, constant and telescopic wall thickness, pipe network design, pipeline economics, transient pipe flow, pumps performance, affinity laws, cavitations and net positive suction head. Introduces drag reduction techniques, thermal hydraulics and natural gas transmission. Prerequisite: MCE 344.

MCE 487.d: Explores classification of turbomachines, dimensional analysis and model testing; basic equations of fluid mechanics and Euler’s theory; incompressible flow turbomachines (centrifugal and axial flow pumps), system matching, performance characteristics and cavitation; hydraulic turbines; compressible flow turbomachines (centrifugal and axial flow compressors), reaction ratio, stage loading, stage efficiency, surge and choking limits; and axial flow gas turbines. Prerequisites: MCE 240 and MCE 341.

MCE 488.d: Explores discretization techniques and solution Undergraduate Course Descriptions algorithms; finite difference solutions to classical model equations pertinent to wave phenomena, diffusion phenomena, or equilibrium, boundary and initial conditions and stability considerations, application into equations of fluid mechanics and heat transfer, using software packages in solving CFD problems. Prerequisite: MCE 325; prerequisite/concurrent: MCE 344.

MCE 490.d: Covers the engineering design process through an open-ended, team-based project of disciplinary relevance. Applies discipline-specific methods and tools to problem identification, definition of objectives and constraints, evaluation of alternatives, and development of a preliminary design. Addresses factors such as sustainability, safety, ethics, economics, societal impact and standards in the design process. Emphasizes the aspects of innovation, entrepreneurship and intellectual property. Develops professional teamwork and communication skills.
